title: Salivary microbiota dysbiosis and elevated polyamine levels contribute to the severity of periodontal disease

sections.abstract:
The oral cavity is a complex environment which harbours the second largest and most diverse microflora after the gastrointestinal tract. The bacteriome in the oral cavity plays a pivotal role in promoting the health and well-being of human beings. Gingivitis, an inflammation of the gingival tissue, arises due to plaque accumulation on the teeth, often leads to periodontitis. Progression of periodontitis resulting in clinical attachment loss, bone loss and eventually the tooth loss is poorly understood. The present study explores the transitions in microbioata, oxidative stress and polyamine levels during the disease evolution which can contribute to developing effective therapeutic approaches.

Saliva samples were collected from seventy-two individuals after procuring informed consent who were either healthy, gingivitis or stage-specific periodontitis patients. Periodontitis stage was confirmed by clinical and radiographic analysis. Microbiota analysis was carried out by 16S rRNA sequencing on the Nanopore PromethIONsystem platform of Oxford Nanopore technologies. Polyamine levels were quantified with fluorescence spectrophotometer. Ornithine decarboxylase quantification was evaluated by ELISA method. Antioxidant levels of the salivary samples were measured by DPPH, SOD, and catalase assays. Autophagy was measured by acid phosphatase assay.

The salivary microbiota exhibited significant changes in their abundance and diversity between healthy individuals and those with conditions such as gingivitis, and chronic periodontitis. A significant increase in polyamines and ornithine decarboxylase was found in gingivitis and various stages of periodontitis. Elevated oxidative stress observed in gingivitis and periodontitis could have resulted in cell death.

The current study shows the role of salivary microbiota and polyamines in gingivitis and different periodontitis stages. The progressive elevation of Streptococcus levels from gingivitis to periodontitis, coupled with polyamine concentrations, may serve as a promising identification marker for assessing the severity of periodontal disease. Insight into the oral bacterial flora and associated physiological changes provide a foundation for targeted therapeutic interventions in gingivitis and periodontitis diseases emphasising the importance of personalised oral health management strategies.

The online version contains supplementary material available at 10.1186/s12903-024-05381-5.

Keywords: Gingivitis, Periodontitis, Polyamines, Oral microbiota, Oxidative stress
sections.introduction:
Gingivitis, characterized by gum swelling, bleeding and redness, represents an initial stage of periodontal disease primarily caused by bacterial plaque accumulation along with hormonal change, diabetes, and smoking [ 16 , 20 , 43 ]. Without appropriate intervention, gingivitis can progress to periodontitis, a more severe condition characterised by a serious inflammation of the gum and supporting structure around the teeth, clinical attachment loss, formation of the periodontal pocket, bone loss and finally tooth loss [ 21 , 44 ]. It adversely affects speech, mastication and esthetics which inturn lowers the quality of life [ 2 ].

Oral microflora comprises of a diverse range of microbial species that harmoniously co-exist with each other and with the host. The external factors such as diet, smoking, and poor oral hygiene can cause dysbiosis with potential implications on oral and systemic health. Over time, the oral cavity has evolved to support a personalized microflora that actively interacts with the host to maintain microbial homeostasis. Host factors can positively impact the microbiome, fostering balance and diversity among species and promoting symbiosis while preventing pathology [ 8 , 25 ]. Conversely, host factors can exert negative effect causing dysbiosis in oral microflora and leading to oral diseases like gingivitis and periodontitis.

Saliva serves as a reservoir of oral bacterial flora and mirrors the overall bacterial composition [ 35 , 38 , 39 ]. Studies using 16S rRNA analysis have identified predominant microbial taxa in healthy individuals, including Actinobacteria, Bacteroidetes, Firmicutes, Fusobacteria , and Proteobacteria . Pathologic conditions like periodontitis is mainly caused by red complex bacteria that converts the symbiotic microbiome to dysbiotic microbial complex hence leading to inflammation and periodontium destruction [ 9 , 18 , 36 , 46 ]. The oral microbiome in periodontitis is characterized by the prevalence of bacterial members of the phyla ; Firmicutes, Proteobacteria, Actinobacteria, Bacteriodetes, Fusobacteria, and Spirochaetes [ 11 ]. Pathogenic bacteria notably Tannerella forsythia, Porphyromonas gingivalis, and Treponema denticola , exhibit high abundance in periodontal disease [ 11 ]. The shift in microbial composition antecedes the clinical manifestations of the disease. Notably, Porphyromonas gingivalis stands out as strongly correlated with periodontitis, disrupting the equilibrium among diverse oral microbiota members and fostering oral dysbiosis [ 12 ].

Polyamines (PA) are organic polycationic alkylamines which is found in all living cells. Putrescine (PUT), spermidine (SPD), spermine (SPM) are integral part of cellular metabolism and play various important roles in cellular function such as cell growth, proliferation, differentiation, and gene regulation. Research studies have documented that PAs in saliva such as PUT, SPD, SPM, and cadaverine (CAD) have great potential to increase the acidity of saliva, influence the composition and metabolic process in it and potentially alter pH balance which may have implications for oral health. Oral maldor and degradation of tissue in periodontitis individuals was reported to be due to the increased CAD [ 24 ].

The oral microbiome can affect the production of PAs. In vitro as well as in-vivo studies showed that Bacteroides spp . and Fusobacterium spp . are involved in the synthesis of PUT and SPD which may contribute to the pathophysiology of periodontitis [ 36 ]. The involvement of oral bacteriome in PA metabolism and its potential implications for periodontal health are areas of ongoing research. Bacteroides and Fusobacterium species have been implicated in PA synthesis, suggesting a plausible connection between the oral microbiome and PA levels. However, further investigation is needed to fully understand this relationship and its relevance to periodontal diseases.

The present work was initiated to assess oral microbiota and PAs in saliva of healthy, gingivitis and periodontitis and to find their correlation to the periodontal health. Understanding these interactions could lead to insights in developing biomarkers for periodontal disease progression and management.
sections.discussion:
Periodontitis is a significant issue affecting approximately 70% of the global population with potential implication on oral health. This condition is characterized by inflammation and damage to the tissues supporting the teeth, alterations in subgingival microbial flora, impaired immune response, and increased oxidative stress. The oral microbial community and its host maintain a homeostatic balance throughout life [ 10 , 52 ] . The dysbiosis within the oral flora can predispose individuals to a range oral infectious [ 23 ]. Variations in the oral microflora occur across different oral niches throughout various life stages [ 30 , 50 ]. The dysbiosis in microbial flora causes the proliferation of pathogenic Porphyromonas gingivalis, Tannerella forsythia, and Treponema denticola , contributing to periodontal disease characterised by gum tissue inflammation [ 22 ].

Previous findings have indicated that Firmicutes and Bacteroidetes increase in periodontitis and shifts in Firmicutes may contribute to the inflammatory processes underlying periodontal diseases [ 14 , 48 ]. Candidatus Saccharibacteria (TM7) possess a negative relationship with periodontitis, playing a protective role by potentially modulating the pathogenicity of their host Actinobacteria and thereby reducing bone loss [ 7 ]. Patients with periodontitis have been linked to alterations in oral bacterial composition, including Streptococcus mitis, S. mutans and S. oralis [ 40 ]. Streptococcal infections of gingiva are rare, but it may cause periodontal damage in aggressive periodontitis [ 19 ] Current study has found that there is a steady increase in the abundance of Streptococcus species in individuals with gingivitis and periodontitis (PI) compared to healthy individuals. Streptococci metabolize dietary sugars to produce lactic acid [ 49 ], which contributes to the demineralization of tooth enamel and the progression of oral diseases [ 15 ]. Furthermore, these bacteria are capable of outcompeting various acid-sensitive microorganisms.While the observed patterns offer valuable insights into potential shifts in microbial communities, further statistical analysis would be necessary to confirm the significance of these findings. This study aims to provide an initial insight into the oral microbial distribution between healthy individuals and dental caries patients.

PAs have been implicated in bacterial pathogenicity and the formation of biofilms [ 4 ]. PAs regulate growth, swarming motility, and biofilm formation in bacteria [ 28 ]. Members of the phylum Firmicutes, such as Streptococcus , are involved in PA production . Earlier research has shown that Streptococcus may possess an inducible form of arginine decarboxylase (ADC) which promotes growth in the presence of polyamines [ 26 , 41 ].

Studies have demonstrated that, P. gingivalis can detect PAs accumulation, respond to arginine levels, and regulate biofilm formation, while also contributing to bone loss [ 17 , 45 ]. It has structures on its surface similar to other microorganisms that form biofilm which could be a reason for the persistent infection in the apical periodontitis lesion. This pathogen is commonly found in the oral cavity and, in some cases, in the lungs of individuals with chronic illnesses, where it can suppress inflammatory responses induced by pathogens or lipopolysaccharides [ 51 ]

ODC gene expression is regulated at the transcription, translation and at the activity levels. The observed differences in the ODC protein levels may be attributable to enhanced translation, as previously reported due to eukaryotic initiation factor 4E [ 37 ]. OAZ negatively regulates protein levels of ODC by directing them to proteasome pathway [ 29 , 32 ]. Given the limited sample size for expression studies, it remains unclear whether changes in ODC, OAZ and SSAT1 expression levels are significant across healthy, gingivitis, and periodontitis groups.

Periodontitis was associated with reduced antioxidant levels compared to healthy controls, potentially contributing to tissue damage. The increased oxidative stress could have triggered the production of PAs in the gingivitis and periodontitis groups. Upregulation of genes associated with PA biosynthetic pathway has been shown to protect against ROS stress and subsequent damage [ 13 , 47 ].

The increased oxidative stress could have lead to cell death in the periodontal disease group which showed significantly higher levels of ACP enzyme. Similar results were obtained in the earlier study where increased ACP activity was correlated to the destruction of bone in the jaw and the worsening of gum disease [ 33 ]. Additionally, research has demonstrated that PAs such as PUT, SPD, and SPM can activate acid phosphatase by reducing the Km value in a dose-dependent manner [ 42 ]. Thus, the relationship between PA and ACP activation indicates a potential mechanism by which PA may influence the ACP activity in gingival tissue and might play a role in the onset and severity of periodontitis.

In summary, maintaining the equilibrium of oral flora balance is vital for oral health, as dysbiosis can cause gingivitis and periodontal conditions. PAs are instrumental in bacterial pathogenicity and the formation of biofilms, while oxidative stress exacerbates tissue damage. Understanding these interactions offers insights into potential therapeutic strategies for managing periodontitis and preserving oral health (Fig. 5 ).
